Picked up the Logitech M240 Silent ($24.99, Best Buy, checkout Sept 2) to replace an MX Anywhere 3 ($79.99) that's been my daily driver for two years. Three weeks in, verdict: for most people, save the $55.

The M240 pairs over Bluetooth only — no Logi Bolt receiver — and connected to my M2 MacBook Air in about four seconds. Scroll wheel is a basic notched mechanism, not the MX's free-spin hyper-fast option, so flying through a 2,000-row spreadsheet takes noticeably longer. Side buttons: two, same as the MX, and both remap fine in Logi Options+. Sensor tops out at 4000 DPI versus 8000 on the MX Anywhere 3, which I never noticed on a desk but did on my lap using my knee as a mousepad — occasional skipping.

Where the M240 actually wins: battery. Logitech rates it at 18 months on a single AA; I'm one month in and the app still shows 100%. The MX charges via USB-C and needs a top-up every 2-3 months with regular use. The M240 is also 15g lighter (78g vs 99g), which matters if you're carrying it to a coffee shop daily like I do.

Build feels cheaper — more hollow-sounding click, visible seam on the underside — but the clicks themselves are genuinely quieter, which I appreciate on calls.

If you're pairing with one machine and don't need multi-device switching (the MX Anywhere 3 handles three via Logi Bolt or Bluetooth with a button press), the M240 covers 90% of the daily use case for a third of the price. I'm keeping the MX for my desk setup and using the M240 for travel.

The sensor is only 4000 DPI vs. 8000 with the MX anywhere 3. I never had a problem on the desk but using my lap, using my knee as a mousepad I had occasional skipping.

M240 does have a battery life advantage. Logitech says 18 months on one AA. I've been using it a month and still 100% on the app. The MX Anywhere 3 charges with usb-c so i have to charge it every 2-3 months with normal usage.
Also, the M240 is 15g lighter. (78 vs. 99g). That might be a big deal for some if you're lugging it to a coffee shop every day like I am.
It does feel a little cheaper. (More "click" hollow sound, has a visible seam on the bottom)

In September 2022, I watched my mother recalculate our grocery list three times at the Kroger on Elm Street before she put anything in the cart. That was the month the Bureau of Labor Statistics confirmed what our family had felt for weeks: inflation had hit roughly 9.1% year-over-year, the highest in forty years. For a household of five in a mid-sized Ohio suburb, that number stopped being an abstraction on the evening news and became a line-by-line negotiation over what we could still afford to eat.

Before 2022, my mother's weekly grocery run cost about $180 and filled two carts. By that October, the same list cost close to $240, and she'd trimmed it down to fit in one. Eggs, which had been $1.50 a dozen, jumped past $3.50 after an avian flu outbreak compounded the inflationary pressure. A gallon of milk went from $2.80 to nearly $4.20. Ground beef, once a Tuesday staple, became a once-a-week treat instead of five nights a week, replaced by lentils and canned beans that my father started buying in bulk from a Sam's Club membership he'd resisted getting for years.

We adapted in small, deliberate ways. My mother switched from name-brand cereal to the store's Kroger-brand version, saving about $1.20 per box. My younger brother, twelve at the time, stopped getting the individually wrapped snack packs he liked for school lunches because the per-unit cost had nearly doubled. We started a small vegetable garden that spring — tomatoes, peppers, and zucchini — not as a hobby but as a hedge against produce prices that had risen almost 8% that year alone.

What struck me most wasn't the math itself but how it reshaped our conversations. Dinner planning, once an afterthought, became a Sunday-night budgeting session with a calculator on the kitchen table. My parents started comparing receipts from Kroger, Aldi, and Meijer, driving the extra fifteen minutes to Aldi because the savings, even $15 a week, mattered.

By early 2023, prices had stopped climbing as fast, but they never fell back. The $240 grocery bill became our new normal, not because we'd gotten used to it, but because there was nothing to return to. That year taught me that inflation isn't just a statistic — it's the quiet erosion of choices a family used to take for granted.
output:
I remember watching my mom go through her mental grocery list three times in September 2022, at Kroger on Elm Street. She didn't even add anything to her cart until then. September was when the Bureau of Labor Statistics finally confirmed for the world (and for us) that we had been in the midst of a historic inflation surge for weeks. The BLS determined inflation was near a 9.1% year-on-year increase (40 year high). What this meant for a family of 5 living in a mid-size Ohio suburb is that the once obscure number on TV during the nightly news became a detailed re-evaluation of our budget, item-by-item, asking ourselves: what can we still afford?

A typical grocery trip for my mom before 2022 was about $180, and involved two shopping carts. Come October, the same list would end up closer to $240. And my mom would downsize to a single cart to handle the new costs. Egg prices, which used to be $1.50/dozen now went well over $3.50, due to the added burden of an avian flu outbreak. A gallon of milk used to be $2.80. Now it was close to $4.20. Ground beef, which we used to have most Tuesday's, was now a once a week "splurge", rather than 5 nights. Lentils, and canned beans entered the fray. My dad started buying bulk lentils and canned goods through his Sam's Club membership, which he had resisted for years.

We adjusted. My mom stopped buying name-brand cereals, and started buying Kroger brand from the store. This was a roughly $1.20 savings per box of cereal. My younger brother (12yo) stopped purchasing those individually wrapped snack packs for school lunch (he loved them), because the price per-pack nearly doubled. We planted a small vegetable garden that spring (tomatoes, peppers, zucchini) not out of a hobby, but more to guard against the almost 8% increase in produce prices for that year.

It wasn't so much the calculations and numbers that stood out to me. It was how these numbers really changed the way we communicated. Dinner became more than just an afterthought. It was now a Sunday night budgeting exercise with a calculator on the kitchen table. My parents would compare Kroger, Aldi and Meijer receipts. The 15 minute drive to Aldi was worth it. Those $15 savings per week added up.

Fast forward to early 2023, prices were no longer on the rapid rise they had been. But they didn't come down. That $240 grocery list just became our new reality. Not necessarily because we grew accustomed to it, but because there was no going back. And it taught me that inflation isn't just a number. It's the subtle (but painful) changes of a family losing access to choices it once had.

The oven (or better, a toaster oven / air fryer) beats the microwave every time — microwaving turns crust into rubbery cardboard because it just heats the moisture trapped in the breading.

Here's what actually works:

1. **Let the chicken come to room temp** for about 20-30 minutes before reheating. Cold-to-hot straight from the fridge cooks unevenly and you end up overshooting the outside to get the center warm.

2. **Preheat oven to 400°F (200°C).** Set a wire rack inside a sheet pan — this is the part people skip and it matters most. Air circulating underneath keeps the bottom from steaming and going soggy, which is exactly what happens if you lay the pieces directly on the pan.

3. **Bake bone-in pieces 15-20 minutes, boneless/tenders 10-12 minutes**, flipping once halfway through. You're aiming for an internal temp of 165°F (74°C) — check with an instant-read thermometer at the thickest part near the bone.

4. **Skip foil or covering it** — that traps steam and undoes the whole point.

If you have an air fryer, it's even faster and arguably crispier: 375°F (190°C) for 4-6 minutes, no flipping needed since it circulates air on all sides. I've done this with leftover KFC-style thighs and Popeye's tenders and both came out nearly as crisp as fresh.

One more trick if the crust still feels a little soft after reheating: pop it under the broiler for the last 60-90 seconds, watching closely so it doesn't burn. That extra blast of direct heat crisps up any spots the convection missed.

Avoid the microwave entirely unless you truly don't care about the crust — even 30 seconds will noticeably soften it.
output:
The oven (toaster oven/air fryer is even better) is vastly superior to the microwave, as microwaving just heats the water inside the breading so you're left with rubbery cardboard crust.

Here's how to do it:

1. Bring the chicken to room temp for 20-30 min before re-heating.  When you go from cold to hot from fridge, it's gonna be uneven and you'll overcook the outside to try to get the inside warmed up.

2. Put oven on 400F (200C).  Put a wire rack on a sheet pan.  (This is the key part that most people forget.)  Having air circulation below prevents the bottom from turning into steam and getting soggy like it will if you put them directly on the sheet pan.

3. Cook bone-in pieces for 15-20 min, and boneless/tenders for 10-12 min.  Flip after half the time.  Shoot for internal temp of 165F (74C)  Test with instant read thermometer in thickest part, near the bone.

4. Don't wrap in foil or cover it.  This will just lock in steam and ruin everything.

If you have an air fryer, this will go even faster and probably be crispier.  375F (190C) for 4-6 min.  No need to flip because the air circulation is going around all sides.  I've reheated leftovers from kfc style thighs and popeyes tenders in the air fryer, and both got almost as crispy as new.

If the crust is still slightly soft after re-heating, the last trick is to blast it under the broiler for the final 60-90 seconds.  Just watch it so it doesn't burn.  This will give it another hit of direct heat to crisp up the spots that weren't as crispy from convection.

The microwave is a hard no unless you just don't care about the crust at all.  Even 30 seconds will make it noticeably softer.

从深圳回长沙定居整整一年了，今天翻账本算了一笔账，跟大家聊聊长沙的真实物价。

先说住的。2023年9月，我们在梅溪湖附近租了个两室一厅，月租2300，同样的钱在深圳宝安只能租个单间。今年3月咬牙买了套二手房，单价1万2，比深圳便宜了整整六倍。

吃的方面真的幸福感拉满。小区楼下的粉店，一碗肉丝粉8块钱，加个蛋10块，老板娘认识我以后还经常多给一勺码子。周末去四方坪夜市，两个人吃小龙虾加烧烤，150块吃到扶墙出。我在深圳科技园吃个普通工作餐都要三四十。

交通成本也低。地铁起步价2块，我办了张卡，一个月通勤花费不到150。打出租车起步8块，上周从岳麓区到高铁站也就40来块。

但也不是什么都便宜。水果价格跟深圳差不多，车厘子还是要五六十一斤。商场里像平和堂、IFS的衣服，价格和深圳没区别，甚至新款还更少。孩子上兴趣班，一节钢琴课200块，也不算便宜。

最大的变化是生活节奏。以前在深圳加班到十点是常态，现在六点半下班，能赶回家吃口热饭。周末约上老同学张磊去湘江边钓鱼，一分钱不花，快乐加倍。

收入确实降了三成左右，但存款反而比在深圳时多了。这个账，怎么算都不亏。
